extracted.intended_audience: students, policymakers, and general readers interested in political philosophy and civil liberties
extracted.subtask_description: Principles for when society or law may legitimately intervene in individuals' conduct. Distinguishes self-regarding from other-regarding actions, specifies thresholds for legal versus social censure, and recommends persuasion/education over coercion in personal matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harm Principle / Justification for Interference
rubrics_metrics.description: As soon as any part of a person's conduct affects prejudicially the interests of others, society has jurisdiction over it; but there is no room for entertaining any such question when a person's conduct affects the interests of no persons besides himself ... In all such cases there should be perfect freedom, legal and social, to do the action and stand the consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interference by society or law is only justified where conduct prejudicially affects others. If conduct concerns only the agent and adults of ordinary understanding, legal and social freedom should be complete; consequences are to be borne by the agent. (This is illustrated repeatedly in the text as the central organizing principle.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between Self-regarding and Other-regarding Conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: A clear categorical distinction: self-regarding actions (which affect only the agent) belong to the sphere of individual liberty; actions that affect others' interests belong to the sphere of social and legal jurisdiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the distinction when judging whether to use social pressure, moral reprobation, or legal sanctions. Examples: being drunk in private (self-regarding) vs being drunk on duty (other-regarding).

rubrics_metrics.name: Social Censure versus Legal Punishment
rubrics_metrics.description: An offender whose conduct is merely self-regarding may be justly punished by opinion though not by law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For personal conduct that harms only the actor, permissible responses are social—opinion, avoidance, warning—not legal coercion. Social penalties should be the natural, spontaneous consequences of the conduct, not inflicted for punishment's sake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Persuasion and Education over Coercion for Self-regarding Virtues
rubrics_metrics.description: Disinterested benevolence should employ instruments other than coercion; education and persuasion, not compulsion, are the proper means to inculcate self-regarding virtues once the period of education is past.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorities and private persons should seek to influence personal conduct by conviction and exhortation. Coercive measures tend to discredit better methods and provoke rebellion among independent characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duties to Oneself are Not Social Obligations Absent Impact on Others
rubrics_metrics.description: What are called duties to ourselves are not socially obligatory, unless circumstances render them at the same time duties to others; 'duty to oneself' beyond prudence means self-respect or self-development, for which one is not accountable to fellows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid converting private self-improvement or prudential choices into matters for legal enforcement unless they simultaneously entail duties to others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral Vices that Harm Others Justify Moral and Legal Reprobation
rubrics_metrics.description: Acts that encroach on others' rights, inflict loss or damage, involve falsehood, unfair advantage, selfish abstinence from defending others, and dispositions leading to these (cruelty, malice, envy, dissimulation, domineering) are proper objects of moral reprobation and, in grave cases, of punishment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When conduct or dispositions translate into harm or breach of duty toward others, harsher moral condemnation and legal penalties are warranted. The text lists specific vices as examples of conduct outside the protected self-regarding sphere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definite Damage or Definite Risk Threshold for Intervention
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever there is a definite damage, or a definite risk of damage, either to an individual or to the public, the case is taken out of the province of liberty, and placed in that of morality or law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intervention should be grounded on identifiable harm or clear risk of harm. Mere conjectural or remote harms do not justify coercive measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on Applying Social Authority Because of Error and Misapplication
rubrics_metrics.description: Interference in matters that concern only the individual's own feelings and circumstances must be grounded on general presumptions, which may be altogether wrong and are likely to be misapplied to individual cases by those no better acquainted with the circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Given the high risk of error and misapplication by outsiders, defer to individual judgment in personal matters unless the harm-to-others threshold is met.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejecting the 'Social Rights' Doctrine as a Justification for Coercion
rubrics_metrics.description: The doctrine that every individual has a vested social right that every other individual shall act in every respect exactly as he ought (i.e., a claim to others' moral, intellectual, physical perfection) is monstrous and would justify any violation of liberty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not accept theories that permit coercion simply because a majority prefers different private conduct; majority taste or moralism is not a legitimate ground for legal compulsion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bad Example Alone Is Insufficient Grounds for Coercion
rubrics_metrics.description: The argument that personal misconduct should be suppressed to prevent corrupting example is weak where the conduct does no wrong to others; often seeing misconduct (and its painful consequences) is more salutary than harmful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not restrict personal liberty solely on the basis that some may imitate; require demonstration that the example produces definite public harm or risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public Opinion Often Enforces Private Tastes Erroneously
rubrics_metrics.description: Public censorship frequently equates the public's distaste with moral law, enforcing tastes and preferences (e.g., religious or sartorial) that are properly private concerns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be suspicious of legislation or social pressure that enforces mere tastes or non-harmful personal practices; check whether the ground is personal preference rather than harm to others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible Collective Regulations Only to Protect Others' Interests (e.g., Sabbath Observance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Customs like Sabbath observance may justify some legal guarantee when necessary to protect the interests of others (e.g., ensuring a common day of rest), but not to enforce religious morality or restrict self-chosen leisure and amusements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorize laws only to the extent they secure legitimate collective interests (such as preventing imposition on others), not to impose religiously grounded moral prohibitions on private amusements or tastes.
